A potentially groundbreaking highlight hidden in the @CMSGov 2027 PFS is also this gem:

A formal request for information (RFI) to overhaul or eliminate the CPT coding system, specifically floating the ideas of using ICD10-PCS to establish payment or using broader categories (similar to how DRGs work for inpatient).

A quick history lesson on CPTs:

-The @AmerMedicalAssn created CPTs in 1966 to standardize medical billing terminology, which otherwise didn't exist at the time.

-In 1983 then-CMS (known as HCFA) made CPTs (as HCPCS) the required code set for Medicare Part B

-In 1992, the AMA created the RUC which is a committee of different specialties that recommend to CMS the RVU values for each CPT. CMS generally took the recommendation, until recent years it started layering in other data to augment it.

-In 1996 HIPAA mandated standardizing electronic transactions and CPT was the required code set for any platform doing physician billing.

The @AmerMedicalAssn makes the majority (55-60%) of their revenue from royalties licensing the CPT code set. Every EHR, billing software vendor, hospital, practice, and payer that processes a claim pays to license the codes — and CMS itself pays to use CPT in Medicare billing. The government mandates the codes... and the AMA collects the licensing fees.

This monopoly has been criticized by @RFKJrHealthSec @SenBillCassidy @RepJamesComer and others...so it feels like this little section II.H in the 2027 CMS PFS is a very interesting move by the Administration to potentially completely revamp healthcare billing...

items.text: @grok @kitdobyns @DrOz @CMSGov Remember that Medicare serves as the basis for private insurance — everything is priced as a percentage of Medicare, so the CMS rate doing down reflects all payors ultimately.

Yes…and the work has only gone up…more metrics, more documentation, more insurance bureaucracy (prior with barely existed in 1993…), more billing complexity (way more ICDs and CPTs now than 1993). Our work has gone UP, which the effective $ drastically down.

No wonder he exited clinical medicine in 2018…🤨

Hey @DrOz,

When you started practicing medicine in 1993, the RVU reimbursement rate was $31.60. @CMSgov is proposing that in 2027, it is $33.40. 

Adjusted for inflation (+132%), 
that’s a 54% cut…

No wonder you quit practicing medicine. The financials don’t make sense. 

Can you tell @CMSGov…oh, wait a minute…

🤔🤨😒

For the @CMSGov proposal to reimburse 50% for same-day E/M and procedure, one nuance for emergency medicine:

This is NOT proposed currently (ahem, @ACEPAdvocacy @ACEPNation) for ED E/M, only O/O E/M (office/outpatient). So the MVC in the ED that gets a sedation/reduction would still be full reimbursement for all CPTs.

Still problematic for outpatient specialties…seems silly of CMS to disincentivize doctors from being like “hey, let me take care of your procedure right now” for the patient…🤨 @AAOS1 @AADskin @aao_ophth @acog @AAOHNS

@CMSGov’s 2027 proposed physician fee schedule is out, and *drumroll please*…

It’s another cut.

1.68% cut in absolute RVU rate ($32.84 down from $33.40)…
But more like 5% real cut when you adjust for the ~3.5% inflation year over year.

Multiplied over ~2.8billion RVUs/year for Medicare FFS, that’s ~$1.55billion being cut for Medicare reimbursement alone — not to mention all the insurances that use Medicare as their benchmark.

Sigh. #healthcare 😞
@TEinsteinMD Indeed…no surprise that insurance is still just denying paying…🤡
@EdGainesIII has a great thread on the new CMS rule for IDR

It always amazes me how little people, doctors included, know about the No Surprises Act (NSA) and IDR (independent dispute resolution).

The TLDR is NSA banned physician groups from billing patients when physicians were out of network and insurances wouldn’t pay. Awesome and the right thing for patients, but then the legislation forced physician groups to recoup money from insurances via forced arbitration (IDR) with very high fees. Even if you won, it was still 6-12mos+ to get any cash in the bank...but the fees and cost get paid upfront…

CMS just issued their updated rule on IDR, which dropped one of those fees by 87%, from $230 to $30. As an aggregate, this drop represents over $500M in fees.

Good news, but obnoxious, since if insurances would just pay physicians in the first place, then the fees wouldn’t exist at all. Cheaper arbitration is still arbitration...

Just another example of health care $ bloat from bad insurance practices. 

https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/federal-rule-takes-aim-health-care-bureaucracy-reducing-dispute-fees-boosting-transparency.html

@UHC announces they’re going to cut prior authorization off 30% of medical services…call me a skeptic, but I think time will tell if they’re just cutting administrative burden on the front end to shift towards financial denials on the backend, which are even harder to identify and subsequently appeal.

Will denials go up? Downcodes? What about retrospective medical necessity review (healthcare already performed, and then after the fact declared to not have medical necessity) or coverage exclusions?

A current 92% prior authorization approval rate means that we already know prior auth is just annoying administrative burden…but the real answer of how impactful this is will lay in the denials rate…

🤔

https://www.unitedhealthgroup.com/newsroom/2026/2026-05-05-uhc-cuts-prior-authorization-requirements-by-30-percent.html

Drug pricing is so complicated and inflated that we’ve had to come up with an entire arsenal of different tricks to try to make them somewhat affordable…@GoodRx, @realDonaldTrump TrumpRx, @markcuban @costplusdrugs , @amazon pharmacy, just to name a few.

But those are all hacks to keep the actually drug price high while just making the payment lower (for those in the know). Imagine if you went to the store, and bread had a sticker price of $100, but with a coupon you could buy it for $2…

Maybe it’s just time to make the sticker price $2. For everyone. Once and for all. 

Read more from me on @Medscape on this topic:

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/trumprx-or-not-trumprx-how-solve-drug-pricing-question-2026a10006g2
